Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I have to be on guard all the time

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: For a 35-year-old single male special education teacher reporting a mugging/robbery, 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile. The other appraisals center on self-blame and persistent danger, but this item implies a salient role failure theme (e.g. partner/parent/protector) that is not otherwise represented in triggers, threat, or memory.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Within Memory, intense shame and intense rage on recall can coexist, but paired with a mugging/robbery and the rest of this profile they pull toward different meanings of the event without enough support elsewhere. Shame would usually connect to strong self-blame/humiliation themes, while rage would connect to injustice/anger themes; the profile does not integrate both clearly.

vignette:
Ethan, a 35-year-old special education teacher, described the last four months of his life as living in a photograph he couldn't turn away from. The trouble began on a Tuesday night in March, walking home from a late parent-teacher conference. Two figures emerged from the alley beside his apartment building. One shouted at him to stop, the sound sharp and ugly in the quiet street. Before he could process the demand, the other man grabbed him from behind, an arm hooking around his throat and twisting his head to the side. The searing pain in his neck was immediate as he was forced to the ground. He remembered the rough texture of the pavement against his cheek and the static-like image of his wallet being pulled from his back pocket. The police who arrived later seemed procedural and distant, their presence feeling more like an indictment than a comfort.

In the weeks that followed, the world became a minefield of reminders. Any sudden, loud noise—a car backfiring, a student having a meltdown in his classroom—would instantly bring the memory flooding back. It wasn't a story he recalled, but a series of high-definition snapshots: the glint of a streetlamp on a belt buckle, the frayed cuff of a jacket, the specific pattern of cracks in the pavement. Each time these images appeared, a hot wave of rage would wash over him, so intense it made his hands shake. He felt a profound fury at his own helplessness, which was almost immediately followed by a crushing sense of guilt. He believed he should have done something different—run sooner, fought back, not taken that route home.

This self-blame began to curdle into a more permanent set of beliefs. Ethan became convinced that he was fundamentally inadequate, that someone stronger or smarter would not have gotten into that situation in the first place. This core belief that he had failed a basic test of survival meant he could never let his guard down again. The world, once familiar, was now a place of constant, imminent threat. He found himself unable to relax, even in his own apartment, and his body was perpetually tense, as if bracing for another attack. At school, a place that had once been his sanctuary, he developed a compulsive need to scan for all the exits the moment he entered any room, from the staff lounge to the gymnasium. His heightened sense of threat also made him more sensitive to the shouting that was an inevitable part of his workday.

The feedback loop was relentless and self-sustaining. His conviction that he was inadequate and had to be on guard at all times (Negative Appraisals → Threat) fueled a pervasive sense of danger that followed him everywhere. This feeling of imminent threat, in turn, made the photographic memories of the assault more vivid and frequent (Threat → Memory). When the snapshots did intrude—the shout, the grip, the pavement—they felt less like memories and more like they were happening all over again, which only intensified his feeling of being unsafe in the present moment (Memory → Threat).

This cycle tightened its grip over the months. The constant state of alert confirmed his belief that he was right to be terrified, reinforcing his sense of inadequacy for not being able to simply "get over it" (Threat → Negative Appraisals). His negative self-appraisals also coloured the memory itself; when he recalled the event, his mind focused exclusively on his own perceived failures, the moments of hesitation and fear, which only deepened his shame (Negative Appraisals → Memory). The chronic, dull ache in his neck, a somatic echo of the attack, became another potent trigger. A simple turn of his head could bring the entire event back in stark, photographic detail, leaving him breathless and enraged in the middle of a lesson plan (Triggers → Memory). He began calling in sick on days he felt particularly fragile, knowing he couldn't manage the noise and unpredictability of his classroom. He finally sought therapy after his principal gently noted his visible distress and exhaustion, expressing concern that he was burning out. Ethan’s hope is not for an absence of memory, but for the photographs in his mind to finally lose their power, to become flat and distant so he can feel safe in his own life again.
